summary: For ages 9–11, compare Heroic-Age polar exploration (c.1897–1922: wooden ships, dog sleds, man-hauling, sextants, furs, and high fatality) with modern polar science (GPS, satellites, icebreakers, ice-core drills, heated research stations, aircraft, and diverse international teams). The core insight is that better tools change not just how safely people work but the QUESTIONS science can ask — shifting from 'can we reach the Pole and survive?' to 'what is happening to the ice and climate, and why?'. Learners compare across clear dimensions (purpose, technology, danger, who takes part), name specific technologies and how each enables survival or new measurement, identify a modern scientist to update the image of who does polar science, and transfer the idea to a new case.
misconceptions: Polar exploration ended with the Heroic Age — it continues as high-tech international science
Modern polar work is just easier sightseeing — it is demanding scientific research, especially on climate
Explorers were all men — today's diverse teams include leading women scientists
New technology only makes old goals safer — it also changes what questions science can ask
The point was always science — the Heroic Age was largely about reaching places first and surviving

activities.title: Then vs Now: a four-dimension comparison
steps: Study paired images or descriptions of a 1911 polar expedition and a present-day research station.
Fill in a four-row comparison table across: PURPOSE, TECHNOLOGY, DANGER, and WHO TAKES PART.
For PURPOSE, write the 1911 goal (e.g. 'reach the Pole first and survive — national glory') beside the modern goal (e.g. 'measure the ice and understand the climate').
For TECHNOLOGY, list then-tools (sextant, dog teams, wooden ship, furs) beside now-tools (GPS/satellites, icebreaker, ice-core drill, heated station, aircraft).
For DANGER, note the high fatality of the Heroic Age versus greatly reduced risk today, and say which modern tool most reduces a given risk.
For WHO TAKES PART, contrast small, mostly nationally organised all-male parties with today's diverse international teams including women scientists.
Write one sentence answering: 'What changed most — the tools or the question?'
activities.insight: Polar exploration did not end with the Heroic Age; it continued and changed. Better tools both reduce danger AND change the questions science can ask — from reaching a place to understanding a system.

activities.title: The purpose-shift arrow and the new question
steps: Draw an arrow from 'reach the Pole & survive' to 'measure & understand the climate'.
Pick one modern tool (e.g. an ice-core drill or satellite) and write the NEW question it lets scientists ask that a Heroic-Age explorer could not.
Explain in two or three sentences how the purpose of polar expeditions shifted, and why the technology made that shift possible.
Answer the lift-the-flap prompt: 'What changed most — the tools or the question?' and justify your choice.

Transfer task: imagine modern scientists suddenly lost GPS and satellites. Explain how much of today's polar work would become more like the Heroic Age again, which jobs would be hardest or most dangerous, and which would still be possible.
activities.insight: Technology does more than make old goals safer; it opens new goals. An ice-core drill makes it possible to read many thousands of years of past climate — a question nobody could investigate with a sextant and dog sled. Because today's science depends on these tools, removing them would bring back many Heroic-Age difficulties.

activities.title: Interview a modern polar scientist
steps: Read or role-play a short profile/interview with a modern scientist — e.g. a glaciologist who reads climate records from ice cores, or a marine biologist studying the Southern Ocean.
Write or speak three questions you would ask about what that scientist studies and how.
Compare that scientist's stated mission with a Heroic-Age explorer's goal, writing one sentence on how they differ.
Name at least one modern polar scientist and say what field that scientist works in.
activities.insight: Today's polar teams are international and diverse and include leading women scientists; the work is science-driven, which is a sharp contrast to the small national, all-male parties of the Heroic Age.

activities.title: Kit out the expedition: then and now
steps: Given a mixed set of items (sextant, GPS unit, dog harness, ice-core drill, fur parka, satellite phone, wooden ship, icebreaker), sort each into THEN or NOW.
For each NOW item, state one thing it lets a scientist do or survive that the matching THEN item could not.
Explain why Amundsen's careful planning and use of dogs is a method/planning difference, not just luck, compared with Scott's man-hauling — using the equipment as evidence.
activities.insight: Differences between eras come from technology, methods and planning, not from early explorers being weak or modern ones being merely lucky.

checkQuestion: A hundred years ago, explorers like Amundsen and Scott raced to reach the South Pole with dogs and man-hauled sledges, and some died trying. Today scientists live and work in Antarctica too. What's the biggest difference in WHY people go there now compared to then, and what lets them survive when the early explorers couldn't? Tell me, and then tell me WHY those things make the difference.
checkAnswer: The PURPOSE changed: the Heroic Age (roughly 1897–1922) was about being first and national glory — reaching the pole itself — whereas modern polar work is about SCIENCE (studying climate, ice, biology). Technology changed survival too: GPS and satellites for navigation and communication, icebreaker ships and aircraft for supply, and heated research stations for shelter mean scientists no longer rely on dogs, man-hauling and sheer endurance, so far fewer people die. Today's teams are also diverse and international (e.g. glaciologist Liz Thomas, marine biologist Sylvia Earle) rather than small national parties of men.
